summary: Informational description of how the Unicode Consortium works, written for people in the IETF. It covers its decision-making bodies and procedures and how the public can access its character encoding and standardization work. It is not a protocol.

eli5.summary: Many internet rules rely on a list of letters from all languages. This explains who keeps that list and how they decide what goes in it.

subtitle: How the Unicode Consortium decides what characters exist

tldr.problem: Many internet standards depend on Unicode for character encoding, but few understand how the Unicode Consortium decides which characters to add, what their properties are, and how stability is maintained.
tldr.mechanism: The Unicode Consortium, a nonprofit corporation, operates through the Unicode Technical Committee (UTC) which meets 4-5 times per year to propose, discuss, and vote on character additions and standard changes, coordinated with the ISO WG2 committee that maintains the parallel international standard.
tldr.outcome: The Unicode Standard and ISO/IEC 10646 are kept synchronized, with stability policies ensuring characters never move, get removed, or change names once published, providing the foundation that allows normalization, IDN, and other protocols to rely on unchanging character semantics.

today: RFC 3718 is Informational and describes the operational procedures of the Unicode Consortium as they stood in 2004. It has not been obsoleted. The Consortium continues to operate under these general procedures; current information about UTC meetings, proposals, and stability policies can be found on the Unicode Consortium's official website.

sections.title: The Unicode Consortium and Its Mission
sections.content:
The Unicode Consortium is a California nonprofit corporation formed to maintain and extend the Unicode Standard. It is not a formal charity but a "business league" bringing together member companies, academic institutions, and governments who commit to supporting the standard's development.

The Consortium has a small permanent staff, a Board of Directors elected annually by full members, and appointed officers who run daily operations. Membership is open to corporations, educational institutions, governments, and non-profit organizations. The Consortium's fundamental purpose is to encode "all the world's scripts" into a single, unified character standard, making it possible for software to handle any human language.
sections.eli5: The Consortium is a club of organizations that agreed to work together to make a master list of all the world's letters, numbers, and symbols. Members meet regularly to decide what gets added to the list.

sections.title: How Decisions Are Made
sections.content:
The Unicode Technical Committee (UTC) is the decision-making body. It inherited work from the earlier Unicode Working Group and has been the technical authority since 1991. Each full member organization appoints one principal and one or two alternate representatives to the UTC.

The UTC meets 4 to 5 times a year for 3-4 days per meeting, with locations chosen by members. Meetings are typically held jointly with the INCITS L2 committee, which is responsible for character encoding standards in the United States. Meetings are generally open to observers, and minutes are posted publicly. A Chair and Vice-Chair appointed by the Board preside.

Discussion focuses on proposals organized in categories: new character additions, preparation of standards and technical reports, changes to character semantics, and extensions to the encoding architecture. Decisions are made by formal motion and vote, where simple motions need a simple majority (over 50%) and precedents (decisions that establish policy) require a two-thirds majority. Proposals can also pass by consensus when all members agree.
sections.eli5: The UTC is like a city council that meets several times a year. Each member organization gets a vote. Committees discuss proposals, and they vote on whether to add new characters or change how existing ones work.

sections.title: Stability Guarantees
sections.content:
The Unicode Consortium adopted Unicode Stability Policies to prevent breaking existing systems. The core rule is unchangeable: once a character is assigned a code point (position in the standard), it will never be moved, removed, or renamed. This promise is absolute.

The policies specify that the canonical combining class and decompositions of characters will not change in a way that affects normalization. This is critical because protocols like International Domain Names (IDN) and web applications rely on normalization being stable and predictable. Each version of the published Unicode Standard is frozen and never changed retroactively.

Character properties such as directionality (used for the Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm) may change between versions as newly encoded scripts are better understood through implementation experience, but this is kept to a minimum and changes are tracked across versions. The Unicode Character Database (UCD)—the repository of character properties and data—is carefully versioned so existing implementations remain stable.
sections.eli5: Once a letter is assigned a number, that number stays the same forever. Old software can rely on this promise. Bonus information about letters (like whether they go left-to-right) might be updated as people learn more, but the core identity never changes.

sections.title: How Characters Get Added
sections.content:
The process for proposing new characters is rigorous and takes years. Proposals can come from national bodies (via ISO), UTC member organizations, or external experts. A standardized Proposal Summary Form is required.

A typical path involves: initial presentation to UTC, review and redrafting, forwarding to WG2 (the ISO committee), re-drafting, a two-thirds majority vote in UTC, forwarding to WG2 with a recommendation, and finally at least two rounds of international balloting. The entire process typically takes about two years.

Proposals rarely get approved on first submission. They are returned with comments and requests for additional information and justification. Proposals for new scripts must be coordinated with relevant user communities, often through ad-hoc expert subcommittees. Multiple rounds of international balloting ensure maturity before final approval. Only when both UTC and WG2 have approved characters do they proceed to the ISO balloting stages.
sections.eli5: Adding a new character takes a long time. A proposal starts, gets discussed, gets sent to international committees, gets voted on multiple times, and gets rejected or improved each time until it's solid enough to accept.

sections.title: Coordination with ISO and Public Input
sections.content:
The Unicode Standard and ISO/IEC 10646 maintain parallel character repertoires, names, and general architecture—they are kept synchronized. ISO/IEC 10646 is maintained by ISO/IEC JTC1/SC2/WG2, composed of national government representatives. Both standards share the policy that characters are never removed or renamed once published.

The Unicode Collation Algorithm (UCA), defined in Unicode Technical Standard #10, specifies how characters should be sorted. It is not part of the Unicode Standard itself but is coordinated with ISO/IEC 14651.

Despite being a membership organization, the Consortium runs an open process. The internal Unicore mailing list carries technical discussion among members and invited experts. The public Unicode mailing list is open to anyone and is publicly archived. Technical proposals are posted to both lists regularly. The Consortium also publishes Public Review Issues to gather feedback on proposals whose impact may be unclear.

Anyone, whether a member or not, can submit character proposals if they are properly justified and documented. The process gives serious consideration to external experts and industry groups.
sections.eli5: Unicode and ISO keep their character lists in sync so everyone is using the same standard. The process is open: anyone can propose a character if they make a good case, and committees discuss it publicly.

items.title: No Removal
items.text: Once a character is assigned, it stays assigned forever.

items.title: No Moving
items.text: A character's code point position never changes.

items.title: No Renaming
items.text: A character's official name never changes.

items.title: Frozen Versions
items.text: Each published version of Unicode is absolutely stable.
